\title{BioQPSO: Bio-Inspired Three-Term Attractors with Adaptive Weight
Scheduling for Quantum-Behaved Particle Swarm Optimization}
\titlerunning{BioQPSO with Adaptive Attractor Weights}
\author{Manav\inst{1}\orcidlink{0009-0005-5197-5195}}

% =======================================================================
\begin{abstract}\sloppy
Quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization (QPSO) samples each particle
around a two-point attractor built from its personal best and the global
best. We study BioQPSO, which adds a third, topology-dependent anchor---a
ring-neighbourhood \emph{bio-leader} chosen by pheromone (AntBioQPSO) or by
fitness with scout re-initialisation (BeeBioQPSO)---and ask whether its weight
$\phi_3$ should be fixed or scheduled. Four schedules (linear, cosine,
stagnation feedback, per-particle) are compared with fixed weights, a
no-bio control ($\phi_3=0$) and a random-$\phi_3$ control.
Twelve algorithms, all implemented in one NumPy code path, are run with
shared pre-registered seeds and a budget of 30{,}030 function evaluations on ten classical functions
and 28 CEC2017 functions ($D=30$, 30 runs).
The results are mixed. On classical functions GWO has the best mean rank
(3.50), QPSO is second (4.50), and the best BioQPSO variants
(AntBioQPSO, FeedbackAda) have rank 5.20; the Friedman test is significant
($\chi^2=43.09$, $p=1.0\times10^{-5}$) but the Nemenyi critical difference
(5.27) separates no BioQPSO variant from QPSO.
On CEC2017 all four Ant-leader variants have a lower mean rank
(3.11--3.79) than QPSO (4.14), but the gap is below the critical difference
(3.15), and GWO ranks 9.96.
In pre-registered controls, no schedule beats the best fixed $\phi_3$ on any
of 10 functions, and the bio-leader beats the no-bio control on only 4 of 10,
below the pre-registered threshold of 5. All BioQPSO variants are poor on
Schwefel. GWO's strong classical results occur on functions whose optimum is at the
origin and reverse on shifted and rotated CEC2017 functions, so they should be read with that caveat.
We conclude that the fixed-weight Ant-leader attractor is a reasonable, low-overhead QPSO
variant whose advantage is visible on CEC2017 but not statistically
established, and that adaptive scheduling gives robustness to the choice of
$\phi_3$ rather than improvement over a well-chosen fixed value.

\keywords{Quantum-behaved particle swarm optimization \and
Adaptive weight scheduling \and Bio-inspired hybridisation \and
Metaheuristics \and CEC2017 \and Feature selection}
\end{abstract}

% =======================================================================
\section{Introduction}
Particle swarm optimization (PSO)~\cite{Kennedy1995} is prone to premature
convergence on multimodal landscapes. QPSO~\cite{Sun2004,Fang2010}
replaces the velocity update by sampling from a delta-potential-well
distribution around a local attractor, leaving one main parameter, the
contraction--expansion coefficient $\beta$. Most QPSO hybrids that
borrow ideas from ant or bee colonies add the bio-inspired operator
\emph{after} the base update (as a perturbation or restart).

BioQPSO instead places the bio-inspired signal \emph{inside} the attractor,
\begin{equation}
q_{i,d}(t)=\phi_1\,p_{i,d}(t)+\phi_2\,g_d(t)+\phi_3\,b_{i,d}(t),\qquad
\phi_1+\phi_2+\phi_3=1,
\label{eq:attractor}
\end{equation}
where $p_i$ is the personal best, $g$ the global best and $b_i$ a
ring-neighbour leader. With fixed weights this is a convex combination of
three anchors. It also removes the random mixing coefficient
$\varphi\sim U(0,1)$ of standard QPSO (Eq.~\ref{eq:qpso-attractor}), so
any difference from QPSO could come from the bio-leader or from the loss of
that randomness; the no-bio control ($\phi_3=0$) separates the two.

\paragraph{What this paper does.}
(i)~It defines the BioQPSO attractor and four $\phi_3$ schedules
(Section~\ref{sec:method}); (ii)~it evaluates them on classical and CEC2017
functions against six baselines under one budget and one code path;
(iii)~it tests two questions: does a \emph{scheduled} $\phi_3$ beat a
well-chosen \emph{fixed} $\phi_3$, and does the bio-leader help at all
compared with the same fixed-weight attractor without it
(Section~\ref{sec:ablation}); (iv)~it reports where the method fails.

\paragraph{Why schedule $\phi_3$ rather than $\beta$.}
Adaptive QPSO work usually schedules $\beta$, the \emph{step size} of the
sampling. $\phi_3$ controls \emph{which anchor} guides the sample and exists
only in the three-term form. $\beta$ decays linearly in all methods here.

\paragraph{Scope.}
The contribution is empirical. No convergence proof is given for the
three-term attractor or for time-varying $\phi_3(t)$. The novelty is
incremental relative to QPSO and to neighbourhood-topology hybrids; we size
it with controls instead of asserting it.

The paper is organised as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related
work, Section~\ref{sec:method} gives the method, Section~\ref{sec:exp} the
experiments, Section~\ref{sec:sens} earlier sensitivity data, and
Section~\ref{sec:disc} the discussion and limitations.

% =======================================================================
\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\sloppy
\paragraph{PSO and QPSO.}
PSO~\cite{Kennedy1995} and its inertia-weight variant~\cite{Shi1998} suffer
from premature convergence and slow fine tuning. QPSO~\cite{Sun2004} models
particles in a delta potential well; Fang et al.~\cite{Fang2010} review
variants. A solitons-based QPSO~\cite{Fallahi2022} adapts $\beta$.
\todo{Add 3--5 adaptive/neighbourhood-QPSO papers you have actually read; verify every DOI.}

\paragraph{Neighbourhood and bio-inspired hybrids.}
ABC~\cite{Karaboga2005} uses employed, onlooker and scout roles; the scout
mechanism is reused in BeeBioQPSO. Continuous ACO
(ACO$_\mathbb{R}$)~\cite{Socha2008} samples from a quality-weighted archive;
AntBioQPSO uses pheromone to pick the neighbourhood leader. Surveys of
nature-inspired methods~\cite{Yang2008} motivate hybridisation but do not by
themselves justify a given hybrid. HSPSO~\cite{Yao2024} combines adaptive
weights, reverse learning and Cauchy mutation for PSO.

\paragraph{Baselines.}
GWO~\cite{Mirjalili2014} and WOA~\cite{Mirjalili2016} are widely used
reference optimizers. More recent optimizers such as the Secant Optimization
Algorithm~\cite{Ibrahim2026} and the Schr\"odinger optimizer~\cite{Hussein2025}
are not compared here. \todo{Add at least one CEC-competitive DE variant (L-SHADE family) as baseline.}

\paragraph{Gap.}
Fixed-weight bio-leader attractors cannot adapt to the phase of the search.
We examine four schedules and whether they add anything over a fixed weight.

% =======================================================================
\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
\subsection{QPSO}
For particle $i$ and dimension $d$,
\begin{equation}
x_{i,d}(t{+}1)=q_{i,d}(t)\pm\beta\,|m_d(t)-x_{i,d}(t)|\ln\frac1u,
\label{eq:qpso-position}
\end{equation}
with $+$ if $u\le0.5$ and $-$ otherwise, $u\sim U(0,1)$, and mean best
$m_d(t)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n p_{i,d}(t)$. $\beta$ decreases linearly from 1.0
to 0.5. Standard QPSO uses
\begin{equation}
q_{i,d}(t)=\varphi\,p_{i,d}(t)+(1-\varphi)\,g_d(t),\quad\varphi\sim U(0,1).
\label{eq:qpso-attractor}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Three-term BioQPSO attractor}
Eq.~(\ref{eq:attractor}) replaces Eq.~(\ref{eq:qpso-attractor}). For
$\phi_k\ge0$ the attractor lies in the convex hull of $\{p_i,g,b_i\}$. This is
a design rationale, not a convergence result.

\paragraph{AntBioQPSO.}
Each particle keeps a pheromone value $\tau_i$ with evaporation
$\tau_i\leftarrow(1-\rho)\tau_i$ each iteration and deposit
$\tau_i\leftarrow\tau_i+\Delta$ when its personal best improves. The leader is
the personal best of the highest-pheromone member of the ring neighbourhood
$\mathcal N_i=\{i-1,i,i+1\}$ (modular):
\begin{equation}
b_{i,d}=p_{\hat k,d},\qquad \hat k=\arg\max_{k\in\mathcal N_i}\tau_k .
\end{equation}

\paragraph{BeeBioQPSO.}
The leader is the best personal best in $\mathcal N_i$,
$\hat k=\arg\min_{k\in\mathcal N_i}f(p_k)$. Each particle has a stagnation
counter $s_i$; if $s_i>L_{\mathrm{scout}}$ it is re-initialised uniformly
(scout phase).

\subsection{Schedules for $\phi_3$}
We schedule $\phi_3(t)\in[\phi_3^{\min},\phi_3^{\max}]=[0.1,0.5]$ and keep the
simplex constraint by redistributing the remainder in the $4{:}3$ ratio of the
fixed configuration $(\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3)=(0.4,0.3,0.3)$:
\begin{equation}
\phi_1(t)=\tfrac47\bigl(1-\phi_3(t)\bigr),\qquad
\phi_2(t)=\tfrac37\bigl(1-\phi_3(t)\bigr).
\label{eq:redistribution}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{LinearAda.}
$\phi_3(t)=\phi_3^{\max}-(\phi_3^{\max}-\phi_3^{\min})\,t/T_{\max}$.

\paragraph{CosineAda.}
$\phi_3(t)=\phi_3^{\min}+\tfrac12(\phi_3^{\max}-\phi_3^{\min})\bigl(1+\cos(\pi t/T_{\max})\bigr)$.

\paragraph{FeedbackAda.}
With a global stagnation counter $s_g$ (reset when $g$ improves),
\begin{equation}
\phi_3(t{+}1)=\begin{cases}
\min(\phi_3(t)+\delta,\phi_3^{\max}), & s_g(t)>W,\\
\max(\phi_3(t)-\delta,\phi_3^{\min}), & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
with $\delta=0.02$, $W=20$ and $\phi_3(0)=0.3$.

\paragraph{PerParticleAda.}
Particle $i$ uses its own counter $s_i$:
$\phi_{3,i}(t)=\phi_3^{\min}+(\phi_3^{\max}-\phi_3^{\min})\min(s_i/L_{\mathrm{scout}},1)$.

\paragraph{Controls.}
\emph{No-bio}: $\phi_3=0$ with $\phi_1{:}\phi_2=4{:}3$ (fixed weights, no neighbour
leader). \emph{Random}: $\phi_3(t)\sim U[0.1,0.5]$ each iteration, to
test whether variation alone, rather than a structured schedule, matters.

\paragraph{Pairing of schedules and leaders.}
In the main benchmark (E1), LinearAda, CosineAda and FeedbackAda use the ant
leader and are compared with fixed AntBioQPSO; PerParticleAda uses the bee
leader (with scouts) and is compared with fixed BeeBioQPSO. The control
experiment (E2) runs every schedule on both leaders so that schedule and
leader type are not confounded.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Unified BioQPSO / AdaBioQPSO}\label{alg:main}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\State \textbf{Input:} $n$, bounds, $D$, $T_{\max}$, schedule, leader $\in\{$Ant, Bee$\}$
\State Initialise $x_i$ uniformly; $p_i\!\leftarrow\!x_i$; $g\!\leftarrow\!\arg\min f(p_i)$; $\tau_i\!\leftarrow\!1$; $s_i\!\leftarrow\!0$; $s_g\!\leftarrow\!0$
\For{$t=1$ \textbf{to} $T_{\max}$}
  \State compute $\phi_3(t)$ (or $\phi_{3,i}(t)$); set $\phi_1,\phi_2$ by Eq.~(\ref{eq:redistribution})
  \State $\beta\leftarrow\beta_{\mathrm{start}}-(\beta_{\mathrm{start}}-\beta_{\mathrm{end}})t/T_{\max}$; $m\leftarrow\frac1n\sum_i p_i$
  \State (Ant) $\tau_i\leftarrow(1-\rho)\tau_i$
  \For{each particle $i$}
    \State $b_i\leftarrow p_{\hat k}$ (Ant: max $\tau$; Bee: min $f(p_k)$ over $\mathcal N_i$)
    \State $q_i\leftarrow\phi_1p_i+\phi_2g+\phi_3b_i$
    \State sample $x_i$ by Eq.~(\ref{eq:qpso-position}); clip to bounds; evaluate $f_{\mathrm{new}}$
    \If{$f_{\mathrm{new}}<f(p_i)$}
      \State $p_i\!\leftarrow\!x_i$; update $g$; (Ant) $\tau_i\!\leftarrow\!\tau_i+\Delta$; $s_i\!\leftarrow\!0$
    \Else
      \State $s_i\leftarrow s_i+1$
    \EndIf
  \EndFor
  \State (Bee) re-initialise particles with $s_i>L_{\mathrm{scout}}$; $s_i\leftarrow0$
  \State (Feedback) update $s_g$ and $\phi_3$
\EndFor
\State \Return $g$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Cost.}
A position update is $\mathcal O(nD)$ per iteration; pheromone and counter
updates add $\mathcal O(n)$, and scouts re-evaluate at most $n$ particles. Total
cost is $\mathcal O(nDT)$ as for QPSO; measured overheads are in
Section~\ref{sec:runtime}.

\paragraph{On convergence.}
Keeping $\phi_3\in[0.1,0.5]$ keeps $\phi_1+\phi_2\ge0.5$ and the attractor
inside the convex hull of three particle-derived points. This does
\emph{not} show that the known QPSO convergence result carries over; no proof
is claimed.

% =======================================================================
\section{Experiments}\label{sec:exp}
\subsection{Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Budget:} $n=30$, $T_{\max}=1000$, 30 independent runs, $D=30$.
 Seeds are pre-registered (\texttt{config/seeds.yaml}) and shared across
 algorithms, so all algorithms start from the same initial population for a
 given run index. Maximum FEs $=n(T_{\max}{+}1)=30{,}030$; BeeBioQPSO scout
 re-evaluations count. This is a \emph{light} budget (the CEC standard is
 $10^4D$ FEs).
\item \textbf{Functions:} ten classical functions (Table~\ref{tab:funcs}) and
 28 CEC2017 functions from \texttt{opfunu}~\cite{opfunu} (F1--F4, F6--F29;
 F5 excluded; see below). Function names and ids should be taken from the library, not
 from the numbering of the original CEC2017 report~\cite{Awad2017}.
\item \textbf{Algorithms (12):} PSO ($w=0.729$, $c_1=c_2=1.494$), QPSO,
 ACO$_\mathbb{R}$ ($q=0.1$, $\xi=0.85$), ABC (limit 30), GWO, WOA (own NumPy
 implementations in the same code path as the BioQPSO family), fixed
 AntBioQPSO and BeeBioQPSO ($\phi=(0.4,0.3,0.3)$, $\rho=0.1$, $\Delta=1$,
 $L_{\mathrm{scout}}=15$) and the four schedules ($[\phi_3^{\min},\phi_3^{\max}]=[0.1,0.5]$).
\item \textbf{Boundary handling:} projection (clipping) for all algorithms; reflect
 and random re-initialisation are tested only in the Schwefel diagnosis (E7).
\item \textbf{Statistics:} primary inference is across functions: Friedman
 test on per-function mean ranks and Nemenyi post hoc,
 $\mathrm{CD}=q_{0.05}\sqrt{k(k+1)/(6N)}$~\cite{Demsar2006}, with $N$ the
 number of functions. Per-function paired Wilcoxon tests against QPSO (one-sided,
 ``better'') use Holm correction~\cite{Holm1979} and rank-biserial $r$; a
 relative improvement below 1\% is called negligible regardless of $p$.
\item \textbf{Pre-registered rule} (\texttt{docs/DECISION\_RULE.md}, committed
 before E1--E3): a schedule is credited on a function only if it beats the
 best fixed $\phi_3$ with Holm-corrected $p<0.05$ and $>1\%$ relative
 improvement; the bio-leader is credited overall only if it beats the no-bio
 control on at least 5 of 10 functions.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Earlier batches.}
The preprint~\cite{Manav2026BioQPSO} and an earlier draft reported two batches
that disagreed for the same algorithm (AntBioQPSO on Levy:
$2.68\times10^{-9}$ vs.\ $1.33\times10^{-1}$). \texttt{docs/REPRO.md} traces
this to one divergent run in the second batch and the absence of shared seeds
and RNG streams. All numbers below come from the single unified run.

\paragraph{Observations.}
(1)~GWO has the best mean rank (3.50) and wins seven of the ten functions
(Sphere, Rosenbrock, Zakharov, Dixon--Price, Ackley, Griewank,
Styblinski--Tang), often by many orders of magnitude. (2)~QPSO is second
(4.50). On Levy its mean ($3.3\times10^{-2}$, std $1.8\times10^{-1}$) is
inflated by outlier runs; ABC achieves the best Levy mean
($4.4\times10^{-11}$). (3)~ABC wins three functions: Rastrigin, Levy and
Schwefel. (4)~Fixed AntBioQPSO and FeedbackAda are the best BioQPSO variants
(rank 5.20), within one critical difference of QPSO. (5)~BeeBioQPSO and
PerParticleAda (ranks 7.40 and 8.40) are clearly weaker, especially on Sphere
and Ackley. (6)~All BioQPSO variants are far worse than the non-bio baselines
on Schwefel.

\paragraph{Caveat on GWO.}
Sphere, Zakharov, Rastrigin, Ackley and Griewank have their optimum at the origin of a
symmetric search space. GWO/WOA-type algorithms are known to favour
search-space centres, and GWO's exact zeros on Sphere and Rastrigin in the
scalability study (Section~\ref{sec:scal}) are consistent with this. GWO ranks
9.96 on the shifted and rotated CEC2017 functions. Classical results for
GWO should therefore not be generalised.
\todo{Add shifted (and rotated) versions of the classical functions to E1 to quantify this effect.}

\subsection{Statistical analysis}\label{sec:stats}
\paragraph{Across functions.}
The Friedman test over the 10 classical functions gives
$\chi^2=43.09$, $p=1.0\times10^{-5}$ ($k=12$). With $q_{0.05}=3.268$ the
Nemenyi critical difference is $\mathrm{CD}=5.27$, and no BioQPSO variant
differs from QPSO by more than CD. With only 10 functions the test has low
power; failure to separate is not evidence of equivalence.

\paragraph{Per function, against QPSO.}
Table~\ref{tab:wilcoxon} (exploratory) lists Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon
results with effect sizes. Holm correction is applied within each function across
the 11 non-QPSO algorithms.

\subsection{CEC2017 (E3, $D=30$, light budget)}\label{sec:cec}
\paragraph{Function set.}
F5 is excluded: in \texttt{opfunu}~1.0.4 the function behind id F5 is nearly
constant over the search domain ($0.5/100$ input scaling), which gave the
spurious value 500.00 for every algorithm in the earlier batches
(\texttt{docs/CEC2017\_CHECK.md}). The remaining 28 functions pass the unit test
$f(x^*)=f_{\mathrm{bias}}$. The opfunu ids correspond to the functions
listed in \texttt{docs/CEC2017\_CHECK.md} (e.g.\ F1 = Bent Cigar, F2 = Zakharov,
F4 = Rastrigin, F9 = Schwefel); the official CEC2017 numbering removed F2, so
opfunu's F22017 is an extra function, not the official F2.

\paragraph{Ranking.}
Friedman: $\chi^2=218.71$, $p=9.6\times10^{-41}$; Nemenyi $\mathrm{CD}=3.15$
($k=12$, $N=28$, $q_{0.05}=3.268$). Table~\ref{tab:cec_ranks} lists the mean
ranks. All four Ant-leader variants (fixed 3.11, Cosine 3.29, Linear 3.39,
Feedback 3.79) rank better than QPSO (4.14), but the largest gap, 1.03, is
below the critical difference, so no separation is claimed. GWO (9.96), WOA
(8.79), ACO$_\mathbb{R}$ (10.64) and PSO (11.00) rank worst. The consistency of
the direction across four variants is suggestive but is not independent
evidence, because the four variants share the ant leader and similar $\phi_3$ values.

\subsection{Controls: scheduling and the bio-leader (E2)}\label{sec:ablation}
E2 runs both leaders with fixed $\phi_3\in\{0.1,\dots,0.5\}$, each schedule, the
random-$\phi_3$ control, the no-bio control and QPSO, on the ten classical
functions (30 runs each).

\paragraph{Implementation note.}
The sweep nominally included $\phi_3=0$, but the schedule class clipped it to
$\phi_3^{\min}=0.1$, so the $0$ and $0.1$ settings are identical. The effective fixed
sweep is therefore $\{0.1,\dots,0.5\}$; the no-bio control, which bypasses the
clip, is a separate run with $\phi_3$ exactly 0.

\paragraph{Q1: does scheduling beat the best fixed $\phi_3$?}
Under the pre-registered rule, \textbf{no schedule is credited on any of the
10 functions for either leader (0/10)}. The fixed-$\phi_3$ landscape is nearly
flat on most functions (Fig.~\ref{fig:phi3heat}), so there is little for a
schedule to exploit. Adaptive scheduling is therefore equivalent to a fixed
$\phi_3$ in this study, with the practical benefit of not having to choose one.

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{phi3_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Fixed-$\phi_3$ heat-map (ant leader, E2): normalised $\log_{10}$ mean fitness per function and $\phi_3$ (green: better).}
\label{fig:phi3heat}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Q2: does the bio-leader help?}
Fixed AntBioQPSO beats its no-bio control on 4 of 10 functions and fixed
BeeBioQPSO beats its control on 4 of 10; both are below the pre-registered
threshold of 5, so \textbf{the bio-leader is not credited overall on the
classical suite}. For both leaders the four credited functions are
Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, Schwefel and Levy (Holm $p<0.05$ with $>1\%$
relative improvement). On the smooth functions Sphere, Zakharov, Ackley and
Griewank the no-bio control is markedly better than the bio variants, so on
those functions the bio-leader hurts. The function-level breakdown is in
Table~\ref{tab:controls}.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Schwefel diagnosis (E7)}\label{sec:schwefel}
All BioQPSO variants are much worse than QPSO on Schwefel in E1. E7 varies the
boundary handler on Schwefel ($D=30$, 30 runs; Table~\ref{tab:e7}). Reflecting
at the bounds improves QPSO strongly (mean $4277 \to 1797$), improves
BeeBioQPSO moderately ($8587 \to 6062$), and improves fixed AntBioQPSO only
slightly ($8050 \to 7669$). It does not help the no-bio ant control or
CosineAda, and random re-initialisation makes every algorithm worse. So the
failure is not mainly a clipping artefact, and it is not removed by switching
off the bio-leader either. One hypothesis is that neighbourhood anchoring
concentrates the swarm in interior basins while the Schwefel optimum lies near
the boundary; the data do not test this.

\subsection{Feature selection (E8)}\label{sec:fs}
Each particle is a vector in $[0,1]^D$ and entries $\ge0.5$ select a feature.
Fitness $f(x)=0.7(1-\bar\alpha_{\mathrm{inner}})+0.3|S|/D$ with an inner
3-fold $k$-NN ($k=5$) computed only on the outer-training split. Outer:
stratified 5-fold repeated 6 times (30 evaluations per algorithm and dataset);
test accuracy with both $k$-NN and RBF-SVM. Datasets: Breast Cancer
(30 features), Wine (13), Ionosphere-synthetic (34) and Madelon-synthetic (500);
baselines all-features and mutual-information top-$k$ ($k=D/4$).
The inner CV uses 3-fold rather than the planned 5-fold for computational
speed; this is a deviation from the pre-registered protocol that may
slightly overestimate accuracy.

\subsection{Runtime (E9)}\label{sec:runtime}
Table~\ref{tab:runtime} gives median wall-clock time (10 repetitions, four
functions, $D=30$, one thread) for all algorithms in the same NumPy code path.
Relative to QPSO, PSO is about 25\% faster, AntBioQPSO about 28\% slower,
FeedbackAda about 26\% slower, BeeBioQPSO about 11\% slower, PerParticleAda
about 88\% slower and GWO about 121\% slower. The PerParticleAda overhead
was traced to \texttt{np.clip} on scalar values in the per-particle $\phi_3$
loop (9.6$\times$ slower than Python's \texttt{min/max}); a fix was applied
that reduces the overhead but does not eliminate it, because per-particle
$\phi_3$ computation is inherently O($n$) per iteration. Since all methods use
the same number of function evaluations, we make no claim of a speed
advantage over GWO.

\begin{table}[t]

\paragraph{FeedbackAda.}
On Sphere the settings $W=20,30,50$ give identical results, which suggests
the stagnation trigger never fires on that function under the shared seeds,
so FeedbackAda there reduces to a fixed decay of $\phi_3$. Differences on
Rastrigin and Levy are within run-to-run dispersion (a few Levy outliers
dominate some means), so no optimal $W$ or $\delta$ can be claimed.

\section{Discussion and Limitations}\label{sec:disc}
\paragraph{What the evidence supports.}
(a)~On classical functions (E1), GWO ranks first (3.50) and QPSO second
(4.50); no BioQPSO variant is separated from QPSO (CD$=5.27$).
(b)~On CEC2017 (E3, 28 functions), the four Ant-leader variants rank above
QPSO (3.11--3.79 vs.\ 4.14), but the gap is below CD$=3.15$.
(c)~Scheduling $\phi_3$ does not beat a fixed $\phi_3$ on any classical
function under the pre-registered rule (0/10), so the default $\phi_3=0.3$ is a
reasonable setting that needs no per-function tuning.
(d)~The bio-leader is credited on 4 of 10 classical functions per leader,
below the threshold of 5.
(e)~AntBioQPSO costs about 28\% more per run than QPSO.

\paragraph{What it does not support.}
Statistical superiority over QPSO on either suite; a speed advantage over GWO;
scheduling over a tuned fixed $\phi_3$; a mechanistic explanation of the Schwefel failure;
feature-selection superiority over QPSO (E8 shows no significant difference on 3 of 4 datasets; ABC alone is significant on Wine).

\paragraph{Threats to validity.}
\emph{Budget:} 30{,}030 FEs is low for $D=30$ and well below the CEC standard;
rankings may change at $10^4D$ FEs. \emph{Origin bias:} classical functions with the optimum at the
origin favour centre-biased algorithms such as GWO; shifted and rotated
variants are needed. \emph{Baseline tuning:} baselines use published defaults,
whereas $\rho$, $\Delta$ and $L_{\mathrm{scout}}$ were examined on the same
functions in the earlier batch, which may favour the proposed method.
\emph{Statistics:} 10 and 28 functions give limited power; 30 runs do not
always characterise heavy tails (e.g.\ Levy outliers). \emph{Benchmarks:}
$D=30$ only for the main results; no composition-function analysis. \emph{Missing baselines:} no CEC-competitive DE variant and no
recent optimizers. \emph{Reproducibility:} seeds and code are public; the
earlier batch discrepancies are documented in \texttt{docs/REPRO.md}.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The three-term BioQPSO attractor with an ant leader and fixed weights is a
coherent, low-overhead QPSO variant. It is not distinguishable from QPSO on
the classical suite and shows a consistent but statistically unsupported rank
advantage on CEC2017. Adaptive scheduling of $\phi_3$ did not improve on a fixed
weight in a pre-registered test, and the bio-leader helps on a minority of
functions and hurts on smooth ones. Schwefel remains an unexplained failure.
The CEC2017 result at the standard FE budget, a $D=50$ study, shifted
classical functions, a CEC-grade baseline and a larger-budget feature-selection
study are the experiments that would settle whether the CEC2017 signal is real.
